title: Models Designed to Forget: Machine Unlearning via Key Deletion
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Forgetting is built into the design: instance-specific memory is separated from the weights, so deleting one key removes a sample without retraining.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, numbered stages, middle panel highlighted in blue
description: Three rounded panels read left to right and are numbered 1 to 3: Training, MUNKEY Unlearning, and Inference. In Training, a dog image becomes a column of colored image tokens z_i. A key/value memory bank M, drawn as two striped stacks labeled K and V, supplies an exemplar token v_i' that is concatenated with the image tokens. The tokens go into a trapezoid transformer f_theta, drawn with a flame icon for trainable parts, which outputs y_i. The middle panel has a light-blue background. It shows the equation M_u = M \ {(k_i, v_i)} and a cartoon monkey with a hammer removing a red-hatched row from the frozen memory stacks. The Inference panel shows a ladybug query, a frozen network marked with a snowflake icon, and k-nearest-neighbor retrieval from the updated memory. A dashed callout shows the ensembling of K predictions as a weighted sum. Orange tones mark training and blue tones mark inference.
caption: Overview of MUNKEY. (1) Training: The learnable exemplar token vi from the memory bank M is concatenated to image tokens zi to predict the label yi. (2) Unlearning results in a simple instance-specific key deletion in M. (3) Inference: For a query xq, the model retrieves K-nearest neighbor tokens from the updated memory Mu and ensembles their predictions for the final output.
abstract: Machine unlearning for vision models is rapidly becoming a practical requirement, driven by privacy regulations, data errors, and the need to remove harmful or corrupted training images. Despite this, most existing approximate unlearning methods tackle the problem from a post-hoc perspective. They attempt to erase the influence of targeted samples through parameter updates that typically require access to the full training data. This creates a mismatch with real deployment scenarios where unlearning requests can be anticipated, revealing a fundamental limitation of post-hoc approaches. We motivate unlearning by design, a novel paradigm for approximate methods in which models are directly trained to support forgetting as an inherent architectural capability. We instantiate this idea with Machine UNlearning via KEY deletion (MUNKEY), a memory-augmented transformer that decouples instance-specific memorization from model weights. Here, unlearning corresponds to removing the instance-identifying key, enabling zero-shot forgetting without weight updates or access to the original samples or labels. Across natural image benchmarks, fine-grained visual recognition, and medical datasets, MUNKEY outperforms all post-hoc baselines. Our results establish that unlearning by design enables fast, deployment-oriented unlearning while preserving predictive performance.
